about: Words for the chain amber_road (cards: Data/encounters/chain_amber_road_793.json; page: Design/content/chains/amber_road.md). Amber from the Ests at Truso, as Wulfstan saw them about 890. Every title, intention, line, option label and outcome of the fourteen cards, an art.<card id> line for each card and one picture for each of the four endings. Wulfstan's own sentences are our rendering of the Old English (texts_793.json wulfstan), not a quotation from any translation. People are called by what they are (the Dane, the steward, the brew-wife) because the engine forges names. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: Sea-stone
A bead-maker sits in a litter of yellow chips, sorting a sack of raw amber into what he can use and what he was cheated with. The second heap is the larger.
This came through three hands before mine. Each hand kept a little and called it weight.
It comes from the Ests. Seven days east of Sliesthorp if the wind holds, the Wends' land on your right hand the whole way, then a river mouth, then a lake. So I am told. I make beads.
They pick it up off the beach after the autumn gales. The old story is that they were surprised anyone paid for it. Somebody has been telling them since.
Is that sea-stone in your boat? Bring it here. I want to see how badly you were cheated, and by whom, because it may have been my cousin.
They have a tongue of their own that nobody learns. But there are Danes on that beach with scales, and Norse will serve you as far as the scales go.
Sit by his bench for the afternoon and watch how he tells good from bad
Buy a sack of his raw amber and have him sort it in front of you
Ask what he would pay for amber brought straight from the lake

He rubs a lump on his sleeve and holds it over the sweepings: chaff jumps to it. He drops a handful in a bowl of brine: the amber floats, the stone and the glass go down. He puts a piece to your lip. Amber is warm. Glass is cold. That is the whole of it, he says, and it took him six years.

He tips your sack out and sorts it as he talks: sleeve, brine, lip. A fifth of it goes on the floor. He does not give the silver back for the fifth. He says you have just bought the cheapest thing he sells, and he does not mean the amber.
Six sacks, he says, clean, inside eight moons. Half as much again as the market gives. He does not offer to tell you how to know clean from dirty, and you did not ask.
A wake on the lake

The beach at Truso is full of boats and nobody is selling. Up in the fort they are drinking, and by the sound they have been at it some time. A Dane with a pair of folding scales in his belt comes down to see who you are.
You have come to a wake. The king of this fort is dead and he is still in his house. He will be there a good while yet. A small man lies a month before they burn him. A king, half a year sometimes.
Until he burns, the king's store is shut, and the king's store is where the amber is. His kin drink and play away what he owned. What you see sold on the beach is gleanings.
And do not go looking for a greater king to complain to. Every fort in this land has its own, and no two of them are friends.
A bead-maker sent you. Seven days, he said? He has never made the passage. He is right, mind. It annoys me.
A stranger at a wake drinks. Then we see what he is.
He will hold out two bowls. Mind which. Here the king and the rich men drink mares' milk. Mead is for the poor and the slaves. And nobody on this shore brews ale. They have never tasted it.
Take the mares' milk, and keep your face still
Take the mead: it is what you know
Send to the boat for the last of your own ale and pour it for them
It is thin and sour and it bites the tongue. You drink all of it. The steward watches your face the whole way down, finds nothing there, and seats you at the upper end, among men who own horses.

The mead is good. They seat you at the lower end, by the door, among men with sand in the seams of their clothes. By the third bowl you understand, without a word in common, that these are the ones who pick the amber up.

Your crew watch their ale go up the hill. The dead king's brother drinks, waits, and drinks again. He asks, through the Dane, what it is made of. Barley. He says they feed that to horses. Then he holds the bowl out to be filled.
The cold house
They take you in to see the dead king. He lies on a bench in his own house, dressed, his weapons beside him, and the room is as cold as the bottom of a well. Your breath shows. His does not.
Ten weeks dead. Smell. Nothing. There is one kin among them that can make cold, and they are sent for when a great man dies.
I have seen her set down two bowls, one of water and one of mead, and both were skinned with ice by morning. Summer or winter. She does not care which.
Go and stand outside a moment. Feel the sun on your neck. Then come back in and tell me how it is done, because I have been here twelve winters and I cannot.
The Dane wants to know how. The Dane always wants to know how.
You drank the milk, so you may stand at his head. That is a place. Do not waste it by touching anything.
Those along the wall are his goods. There is less each day: it goes in drink and on the gaming board. Lay something by him if you like. It will be drunk or ridden for with the rest.
Lay silver at the dead man's feet, as his own people do
Ask the woman, through the Dane, how the cold is made
Stand where you are told and keep your hands to yourself
You weigh out fifteen pennies' worth and lay it by his feet. Nobody thanks you. The old woman looks at the silver, then at you, for about as long as it takes to count a stranger.

She lifts a board under the bench. Below is a pit lined with moss and straw and packed with lake ice, cut at midwinter, grey and hard as stone. That is half, the Dane says for her. She puts the board back. The other half is in a pot she does not open.
She says something short. The Dane does not put it into Norse. After that you are given a place by the door, where it is warmer, and where you can see nothing.
You stand and count. A heap of raw amber. Marten skins tied in forties. A sword. Silver cut small. A bridle with silver on it. A kettle. The Dane says there were two more heaps at the last moon.
Three heaps
A woman has spread a cloth on the shingle: yellow lumps in three heaps, wetted so they shine. She names one price for all of it. The Dane holds his scales and looks at the lake.
Sea-stone. West shore, after the storm. All good. Weigh it, Dane.
I weigh. I do not say what is on the pan. That is how a Dane keeps a house on this beach, and she knows I keep to it.
They say the Ests do not know what the stuff is worth. That was true in somebody's grandfather's time. Now they know to the grain what a stranger does not know.
You pick it up like a man who has sat at a bead-maker's bench. Good. Then this is a fair fight, and I shall enjoy it.
One word for nothing, because I liked how you tied up your boat. Half the trade here is knowing what is in the heap.
The men you drank mead with are down the shore, picking over last night's weed. They sell too. Not so prettily laid out. I did not tell you that.
Test it piece by piece: sleeve, brine and lip
Buy by the look of it
Buy nothing. Ask her to show you what she would not buy herself
Go round her: the men from the low bench sell on the shore itself

A third of her middle heap is pine resin boiled hard, and two fine pieces are yellow glass, cold on the lip. She watches you find each one. Then she laughs, sweeps them into her apron, and fills four sacks with true stone at the price she named for the false.
You point at the dullest heap because the shiny ones look too willing. She stops smiling. Four sacks, and all of it draws chaff when the Dane, who cannot help himself, rubs a piece on his sleeve.

On the boat you try a piece on your tongue and it tastes of a pine wood. Resin, most of it, and some glass. One sack in four is true. When you go back she shows you, kindly, how you could have known: sleeve, brine, lip. She does not give back the silver.

She is delighted. She rubs, she floats, she holds pieces to your lip like a mother feeding a child, and names each thing in her own tongue until you can say it. You leave with empty hands and a morning's worth of her words.

Down the shore three men are raking weed with forked sticks. They sell as it comes, sand and all: nobody has had time to cheat with it. Five sacks. The woman on the cloth watches you carry them past and says one word, which you do not yet know.
Every tongue burns
A Frisian from the Weser mouth has died of a fever in the Dane's guest house, a very long way from a priest. His son comes to you because you are the only other baptised skipper on the lake.
They say he must be burned. Every man who dies here is burned, whatever tongue he spoke. And if one bone of him is found unburnt, there is a great atonement to pay.
He was baptised. He wanted to lie in earth and get up out of it on the last day. I promised him earth. I did not know then what I was promising.
It is their law, and it is my house he died in. If a bone of him turns up whole, I am the one who pays, and it would buy that boat of yours twice. I like the boy. I like my house more.
The fire is no shame. We give it to kings.
If you mean to row a dead man down the lake tonight, do not tell me. And know that the fishermen here do not sleep, and they count boats.
Take the body out by night and bury him in the sand of the spit, by the sea
Stand by the son at their fire, and say the prayers you know
Pay the atonement beforehand, so that nobody rakes the ash too closely

Down the lake with muffled oars, out by the river, and onto the long spit before light. You dig above the weed line and tie two pieces of driftwood for a cross. The son gives you what his father had on him, and a riddle the old man was fond of, about a thing that was water and will be water again.

A fishing boat lies across the river mouth, and then three. Nobody is struck. The dead man goes back up the lake and burns next day with everyone watching. Your share of what the Dane must pay is sixty pennies' weight. The son says you tried, and means it.

The Ests burn him well, with his knife and his cloak, as they would one of their own. You say the Our Father and the Creed, the son says them after you, and your crew stand a long way back. Afterwards the women rake the ash for bone and find none. The steward nods to you as to a man who can be taken places.

The steward weighs your silver, and the women who rake the ash rake it quickly. One small bone goes home to the Weser inside the son's shirt, to lie in earth. He gives you his father's riddle for thanks: a thing that was water and will be water again.
The day is named
The king will be burned at the second new moon from now. The steward has begun to divide what is left of his goods into five heaps, and the fort has begun to talk about horses.

On the day, they lay his goods along the road in heaps. The biggest a mile from the fort, the next nearer, the smallest by the gate. The riders start five or six miles out. First horse to the far heap takes it, and so on inward.
Anyone may ride. Strangers too. That is why a fast horse costs more on this shore than anything else with legs, and why the Wends keep their good ones at home.
The far heap is sea-stone, marten, and his silver. Tell your friend. He looks like a man who counts.
The barley drink. Bring more for my brother's burning. Bring someone who knows how it is made.
He means it. Nobody brews here. Honey is cheap and barley is horse feed. A woman from the west who can brew would be a wonder, and wonders are well paid at a burning.
Two moons. Time enough to see Sliesthorp and be back, if you do not stop to argue with anyone on the way.
Say you will be back with a horse
Say you will be back with ale and a woman who can brew it
Say only that you will be there

The steward holds up one finger, then two: one horse, twice the price. The Dane says that is his opening, and that a horse which has stood seven days in a boat should be walked a week before anyone sits on it.
The king's brother has the Dane say it twice so there is no mistake: malt, six sacks, at double, and the woman. He has no word for malt. He says the barley before it is the drink.
The steward shrugs, then thinks better of it and asks for cloth: four bolts of the Frisian stuff, for cloaks at the burning. He will pay over the market for it. A wake uses up cloaks.
The grey and the brew-wife

Behind the landing a Jute is walking a string of horses, one of them a lean grey that the others give room to. Next door is an alehouse where the ale is good and the woman who makes it is not pleased with her life.
The grey. Do not look at the others, they pull carts. He was bred on the heath and nothing has passed him yet. I have stopped racing him. Nobody will bet.
For the Ests? Then you know why I am not ashamed of the price. Sell him there on the morning of a burning and you could buy my whole string and me with it.
He has never been in a boat. Lay him down on straw, tie a cloth over his eyes, and put a man at his head who is not afraid of him. If the man is afraid, the horse will know before the man does.
A whole people that has never tasted ale. And a king who pays. I have brewed in my husband's brother's house since my husband died, and he drinks the profit. I can be in your boat tonight.
I want malt of my own choosing and a cauldron that has never had fish in it. And a share. Not a wage. A share.
East? There is nothing east but Wends and honey. Drink up. If you ever find a place that wants a brew-wife and has no brother-in-law in it, come and tell me.
Buy the grey at his price
Take the brew-wife east, for a share
Take both: the horse in the bottom of the boat and the woman on top of the malt
Not now

Two hundred and forty pennies, which is two horses. He goes into the boat sideways, on straw, blindfold, with your steadiest man at his head. The Jute watches from the bank and says he will miss the horse and not the argument.

She comes down at dusk with a cauldron, two sacks of malt she has smelt every handful of, a bundle of bog myrtle, and nothing else. She does not look back at the house. She sits on the malt and asks which way is east.

The horse lies in the bottom on straw with a cloth over his eyes. The brew-wife sits on her malt above him and tells him he is a fool to be afraid of water. By the second day he will take barley from her hand and from nobody else's.
You look at the grey a while. The Jute lets you look. The moon is getting on, he says, and so is the horse.
The gate on the water

The Wends' land has lain to one side of you for three days. Now a long low boat puts out from it with more oars than you have men, and a man in her bow holds up an open hand, which may mean peace and may mean five.
This water has a lord. The lord has a gate. I am the gate.
Swear on the water that you carry nothing for the king of the Danes. Then give what a guest gives, or do not. I remember both kinds.
A horse. In a boat. Going east. I know where that horse is going, Frisian, and I know what he is worth there. Be glad I am an honest gate.
Sea-stone from the Ests. They kept you waiting, I can see it in your beard. They keep everyone waiting. It is the only thing they have plenty of besides honey.
Heave to and swear on the water, as he asks
Heave to, swear, and give a guest's gift for his peace this season
Keep the sail full and do not stop

You put your hand in the sea over the side and say you carry nothing for any king. He watches the hand, not your face. Then he drinks a cup of whatever you have, makes no remark on it, and lets go your gunwale. It has cost the afternoon.

You swear, and weigh him fifteen pennies' worth. He weighs it again on scales of his own. Then a crock of honey comes back over the gunwale, because a guest's gift is answered. Until the leaves fall, he says, his boats will know yours.

The wind is on your side of the argument. Their oars keep pace for as long as a man can hold his breath, and then they do not. The man in the bow lowers his hand. He does not look angry. He looks like someone making a note.

The wind drops behind the point, and oars do not need wind. He comes over your side, takes his gift himself, and counts generously. Forty pennies' weight. Next time, he says, swear first. It is cheaper, and the water likes it.
The mile

The heaps are out along the road: the smallest by the gate, the largest a mile off where the road tops the rise. Five miles beyond that, every fast horse in the land is being walked in circles. The dead king is still in his house. He goes to the fire when the last heap is taken.
First to the far heap takes it, the next takes the next. The man who comes last to the gate heap gets a cloak and a kettle and is laughed at until spring.
By tonight he will own his weapons and the clothes he lies in, and those burn with him. They think it a clean way to finish. Twelve winters here, and I have come round to it.
A stranger may ride. A stranger may win. A stranger may not complain.
Your horse has been looked at by everyone who matters. Two of them asked me his price. I said you had not come seven days in an open boat to sell.
Her ale has been working three days in my storehouse and it smells right. She says if one more of the king's kin opens that door to look, she is going home.
You brought yourself. Well. Somebody has to stand at the gate and say afterwards who was first.
While they ride, nobody watches the near heaps but the dead man's women. Do not let me see you think it. A thief at a burning pays more than silver, and so does the man whose guest he is.
Ride for the far heap
Have the ale carried up to the fire
Stand at the gate with the Dane and watch
While every eye is on the road, lift what you can from the near heaps and be on the lake by dark

You remember very little of five miles. A ditch. Somebody's elbow. The horse deciding, somewhere past the second heap, that he did not care to see another horse's tail. Then the rise, and a heap of amber and marten and cut silver with a bridle on top, and nobody there before you.

He runs like a horse that has spent seven days lying in a boat: well, and a little late. Three are past the rise before you. You pull up at the heap by the second ditch, which is a sack of sea-stone and some good cloth, ahead of two kings' sons. Nobody laughs.

The cask goes up to the fire on a pole between two of the king's kin. The brew-wife walks behind it with her ladle like a priest with a cross. By the time the last rider is in, there is a crowd about her three deep, and the mead is standing unpoured.

From the gate you see dust, then horses, then one horse. A boy on a dun mare takes the far heap and stands on it, howling. The Dane names each rider as he comes in. At dusk they carry the king out and burn him, and the fort is quiet for the first time since you came.

The women are watching the road like everyone else. A sack of sea-stone and a bundle of marten go under your cloak, and you are on the lake before the first horse tops the rise. Behind you somebody begins to shout, in the Dane's voice, and not at you. At him.

An old woman you took for part of the wall has you by the wrist, and she is one of the cold-making kin, and her hand is like the room. They take back what you lifted and eighty pennies' weight besides. They do not kill a thief at a burning. They walk you to your boat. The Dane does not come down.
The Frisian on the horse
The king burned at dusk with his weapons and his clothes. This morning the women rake the ash for bone, and your horse stands at the Dane's door with half the fort looking at him.
The far heap. Sea-stone, marten and his silver, and you a man who had not sat a horse since harvest. They will sing about the horse. You they will call the Frisian who was on him.
Fourth. The heap by the second ditch. Nobody laughed, and you came in ahead of two kings' sons, who are over there not looking at you.
The horse. Say what you want for him.
He means anything. A horse that has run at a king's burning is worth more than the heap he ran for, and there will be another burning. There is always another burning.
You rode for my brother. While I sit here your boat is a guest's boat at this fort, and your son's after you. Here is my hand on it.
Take the far heap home, and keep the horse
Take the far heap, sell the king the horse, and ask for ground by the lake
Take your heap, and sell the king the horse that came in ahead of two kings' sons
Take your heap and the king's hand, and keep the horse for the next burning

Fourteen sacks of sea-stone, four forties of marten and the dead king's silver go down to the boat, with his bridle on top, which you do not sell. The horse goes aboard last and lies down without the blindfold. The new king takes your hand in front of the fort. The Dane says he has never had a guest who cost him so little and was worth so much.

The king weighs out silver for the horse until the Dane tells you, in Norse, to stop looking surprised. Then the king walks to the shore with a stick and scratches the corners of a house plot next to the Dane's. The heap goes aboard. The grey watches you go, from a king's stable, eating barley.

Six sacks of sea-stone, and for the horse rather more silver than he cost. The king takes your hand as well. It is the horse he wanted, but it is your hand he took, and at this fort that is remembered longer.

Eight sacks, a forty of marten, and a gift of cut silver from a king who admires a man that will not sell. He takes your hand. The grey goes back into the boat. Next burning, the Dane says, walk him two weeks first, and you may not need my scales again.
Neither milk nor mead

They drank mead at the burning and mares' milk at the high bench, as they always have, and then they drank the brew-wife's ale until the cask sucked air. This morning the dead king's brother, who is king now, has sent for her and for you.
A king drinks milk. A slave drinks mead. This is neither. I can give it to whom I like and insult no one. Do you know what that is worth to a man with forty cousins?
He wants a brewhouse inside the palisade and me in it. I said: malt. He said: what is malt. So I shall be here some time.
As long as anyone remembers, a man could say of the Ests that they brew no ale. He will have to find something else to say about them.
Barley was horse feed here at the last moon. This morning it has a price. I would buy before the next fort hears of it.
They have no word for it. They are calling it by their word for mead and pulling a face to show they mean the other one. I shall teach them a better word when I have learned a worse one.
Leave her here with her share and a brewhouse, and take the malt trade
Take the king's thanks in amber now, and his peace on your boat
Ask for the king's hand between his house and yours, and first pick of each winter's amber

The king's men are cutting posts before noon. She has a house inside the palisade, a share, no brother-in-law, and the key of the store where your goods will lie. Twelve sacks of sea-stone and the king's silver go aboard, and an order for twenty sacks of malt at double. She walks you to the boat and tells you which malt.

Thirty sacks. The steward weighs them himself, and the king lays his hand on your stem in front of the fort: this boat owes no gift here. The brew-wife is already arguing with him about where the brewhouse door should face. She seems to be winning.

The king takes your hand at the gate, with the fort for witness. Each spring, when the winter's sea-stone comes in off the west shore, your boat is weighed before the others. Sixteen sacks and his silver go aboard as a beginning. The Dane says he has waited twelve winters for that hand and you got it with a cask.
The store opens
The king burned at dusk. This morning his store is open, the steward sits before it with the Dane's scales, and the lake is full of boats that waited as long as you did.
Now you see what the waiting was for. A year of sea-stone off the west shore, and they sell it in three days, because they want the store empty before the next fort comes to count it.
You came to the wake. You drank. You kept your hands still. What you won at the board is counted. Weigh first.
The cold-wife told him you laid silver by the dead man before anyone asked it of you. That is why he says weigh first. She does not often speak for a stranger.
And sell that horse before you go. There are men here who would give a daughter for him this morning, and he is eating my thatch.
My father's buyers on the Weser will take all the sea-stone one boat can carry, every year. They need a man who knows this lake. I know it now. And I know you.
I am not young, and a house on this beach wants a boat that comes back every year. Yours could be the boat my store waits for. Think about it while he weighs.
Buy at the first weighing, and take the Dane as your man on the lake
Take your winnings in amber, and have the Dane's boy show you every bar from the river mouth to the lake
Go in with the dead Frisian's son: his father's buyers, your knowledge of the lake
Ask the cold-wife's price for a chest of her packing in your hold

Twenty-six sacks at the first weighing, the best of the store, for a hundred pennies' weight and what you won at the board. The Dane puts his hand in yours over the scales. From now on his store holds your goods through the winter, and he buys for you when the price is asleep.

Twenty sacks. Then two days in the Dane's small boat with his boy at the oar: the bars at the mouth of the Wisle, the broad water they call the Ests' mere, where the little river comes in from the east, and which reed bed hides the channel up to the lake. You could find it now in fog.

You cut a stick between you and each keeps half: his buyers, your lake, one boat each, gain and loss shared. Sixteen sacks go aboard and the silver from his father's last sale. He sails west with a bone or a grave to tell his mother of, and your name with it.

Twenty-two sacks, won and weighed. Then the old woman comes down to the boat herself and packs a chest: moss, straw, grey ice, and a layer of something she turns her back to put in. Butter will keep a month in that, the Dane says for her. Do not open it to look. She knows you will.
A handful of the lake
A Gotland boat came in from the east two days before you. By the time you make fast, the bead-makers' row knows what a Frisian did at a king's burning on the Ests' lake.
The Dane who kept the guest house paid the atonement for you. They took his scales, his store and the timbers of his house. He is at Grobin now, weighing for another man.
And they hold strangers to the beach now. No stranger in the fort. No stranger at a wake. No stranger on a horse. No other shore gave us that, and it is gone.
They let you walk to your boat because a thief at a burning is unlucky to kill. Not for anything you said to them.
I do not ask where sea-stone comes from. I ask what it weighs. But I will say this once: you had the whole lake, and you took a handful.
Sell the bead-maker what you know and what you took, and let him do your buying in the east
Pay the Gotlander to show you the Curonians' shore: they have amber too, and have not heard of you
Send the whole atonement east with the Gotlander, and more, in the Dane's name

The bead-maker pays well for what you can tell him: when the store opens, what the gatherers take, which heap is resin. He will buy in the east through other men and work what comes for your house. He weighs the silver twice. He does not offer you ale.

The row pays for what you know of the lake. The Gotlander takes his own pay in the same kind, and draws the Curonians' shore for you in spilt ale on the bench: north past the long spit, five forts, a river with a market up it. They are worse than the Ests, he says. You will get on.

The Gotlander looks at the silver, then at you, then weighs it. At the turn of the year word comes back. The Dane has his timbers and his scales again and will hold your goods. Strangers may ride again. You yourself may come as far as the beach, and no step further, while anyone lives who was at that burning.
Lands to port, lands to starboard

An Englishman is back from the Ests' lake with a string of rough amber round his wrist and a great deal to say. He means to tell all of it to his king. First he wants to tell it to someone who can say whether he has it right.
Seven days and nights from here to Truso, and the ship running under sail the whole way. The Wends' land to starboard. To port Langaland, Laland, Falster and Scania, and all those belong to Denmark.

Then the Burgendas' land to port, and they have a king of their own. Then Blekinge, More, Oland and Gotland to port, and those belong to the Svear. And the Wends still to starboard, as far as the mouth of the Wisle.
The Ests' land is very large, with many forts, and in every fort a king. There is a great deal of honey, and fishing. The king and the richest men drink mares' milk, the poor and the slaves mead.
And no ale is brewed among the Ests. But there is mead enough. I looked. I am a thorough man where ale is concerned.
And they brew ale there, at the one fort, which I had not looked for. They say a Frisian's brew-wife taught them in their grandfathers' time. They are still pleased about it.
When a man dies, his goods are laid in heaps along a mile and ridden for, and the swiftest horse takes the most. Strangers ride for it too, and take it. I saw it done. I did not ride. I have a wife.

They ride for the dead man's goods, I was told. I was not let see it. No stranger goes past the beach there now, for some thief in their grandfathers' time. A Frisian, they say. I do not say he was kin of yours.
They showed me the rise where a Frisian's grey took the far heap, long ago. They still name the horse. Was he of your house? Then I shall say I have met the horse's people.

And there is a kin among them that can make cold, so the dead lie long and do not rot. Set down two vessels of ale or water and they freeze both, summer or winter. I saw the man. He had been dead since the thaw.
He tells it the same way every time, lands to port and lands to starboard, like a man telling knots on a rope. I have stopped mending it. The king likes a thing plain.
Hear him through, and put him right where your house knows better
Tell him what your house knows of the bars at the river mouth, for a price
Let him talk, and tell him nothing: the road is your house's

It takes the afternoon. You mend one thing: which river loses its name to the other where they meet in the mere. He thanks you gravely and tells it wrong again. The clerk, who has it all on wax, lets you take a fair leaf of it for your chest.

He pays without haggling, like a man spending for a king, and the clerk writes down the bars as you give them. Then he leaves them out, because the king will not want bars. You have the silver and a leaf of the telling.

He talks until the light goes and needs nothing from you but your ears. In the morning he sails for England. Whatever is told of the Ests' lake after this will be his telling, and your house will not be in it.

A workshop booth by the landing at Ripa or Sliesthorp, afternoon light through a wattle wall: a Danish bead-maker in a leather apron sits at a low bench among yellow chips, rubbing a lump of raw amber on his wool sleeve; a bowl of water with pieces floating in it, a bow-drill, strings of finished beads on a peg.

The beach at Truso on its lake, a still grey day: a dozen boats drawn up and no goods laid out; on a low rise behind, a timber fort with smoke and many people; in front a broad Dane with folding scales in his belt and beside him a Prussian steward holding out two wooden bowls, one white with milk, one dark with mead.

Inside a dark log house at Truso, light from the door only: a dead king lies dressed on a bench with a sword and spear beside him; frost on the wall posts and the watchers' breath showing; an old woman in a grey shawl sits by two bowls skinned with ice; heaps of amber, furs and a silvered bridle along the wall.

The shingle at Truso, morning sun on the lake: a Prussian woman kneels behind a cloth with three wet shining heaps of yellow lumps; the Dane stands with his scales held up and his eyes turned to the water; far down the shore three small figures rake seaweed with forked sticks.

The Dane's guest house at Truso by rushlight, night: a dead Frisian merchant laid on a bench under his cloak, a small wooden cross on his chest; his young son stands with his hand on the body; in the doorway the Prussian steward and the Dane, and through the door, the dark lake with one fishing boat on it.

Before the fort gate at Truso, bright afternoon: the steward divides goods into five heaps on the grass, amber, bundled furs, cut silver, cloth, a kettle; the dead king's brother, bare-headed with a neck ring, points down a straight road that runs away over a rise; boys lead two horses past.

Behind the landing at Sliesthorp, a windy day: a Jutish dealer holds a lean grey horse by the halter while cart horses stand aside; in the doorway of the alehouse next door a strong Danish woman with her sleeves rolled leans on a mash paddle, watching the skipper and the horse.

The southern Baltic, a low wooded shore to one side, flat evening light: a long low Wendish boat with many oars lies across the bow of a small sailing boat; a man in her bow holds up one open hand; in the small boat a horse lies blindfold on straw among sacks.

The road from the gate of Truso at midday, seen from the gate: heaps of goods at intervals along a straight mile, the smallest near, the largest on the rise; far off a cloud of dust and the first horses; a crowd along the palisade, the Dane and the skipper at the gatepost, women standing by the near heaps.

The morning after, before the Dane's house on the beach: a lean grey horse, still dusty, tied at the door with a ring of Prussians admiring him; the new king holds out his open hand to the skipper; behind, a thread of smoke from a burnt-out pyre and women bent over the ash with rakes.

Inside the palisade at Truso, morning: an empty cask on its side with a ladle on it; the Danish brew-wife, arms folded, faces the new king, who holds a bowl upside down to show it is empty; behind them two men already setting corner posts for a new house; the Dane watching with his hand over his mouth.

The king's store at Truso thrown open, clear morning: sacks and baskets of amber carried out into the light; the steward seated on a stool with folding scales raised, the Dane at his shoulder; a line of foreign skippers waiting, Danes, Gotlanders, a Frisian at the front; the lake crowded with boats behind.

The bead-makers' row at Sliesthorp, a dull day: a Gotland skipper sits on a bench drawing a coastline in spilt ale with one finger; a bead-maker weighs silver without looking up; the skipper of the small boat stands apart with a sack at his feet, and people in the row behind have stopped work to look at him.

The jetty at Sliesthorp, about the year 890, late light: an Englishman of forty with a trimmed beard, a sea cloak and a string of rough amber round his wrist counts lands off on his fingers; a young tonsured clerk beside him writes on a wax tablet; the listener, a Frisian skipper, sits on a mooring post with his arms folded.

Ending picture, the stranger who rode: a grey horse standing alone on a heap of amber, marten skins and cut silver on a rise in the road, a silvered bridle hung on his neck, the fort small in the distance.
Ending picture, the guest who learned: a pair of folding scales in balance, raw amber in one pan and cut silver in the other, on a boat's thwart; the lake of Truso and its fort behind.
Ending picture, ale among the Ests: three bowls on a bench in a Prussian hall, one of white mares' milk, one of dark mead, and between them one of brown ale with a head on it, a ladle laid across.
Ending picture, the thief: an empty beach at Truso with a line of stakes driven between the boats and the fort, and on the near side one small heap of amber that nobody has come to buy.
